report.verdict: Latin America's 2030 story has split in two. The forecast houses still print a region of $51bn total GGR by 2030 (H2 Gambling Capital, Apr 2026) and $12.3bn of regulated online GGR by 2028 (Vixio), with a $467.6m online-poker niche (GVR) — but every one of those numbers pre-dates Brazil's MP 1.394/2026, which extinguished all 85 federal fixed-odds authorisations from 6 Oct 2026 and removed roughly half of the region's regulated online GGR (R$36.9bn / ~$7.2bn in 2025) at a stroke. Until Congress and the courts settle Brazil's fate, the investable regulated pool is Mexico, Colombia, Peru, Argentina's provinces and (eventually) Chile — a ~$5–7bn market with rising tax takes — while Brazilian demand migrates offshore.

summary: **Two-speed region.** H2 Gambling Capital's 30 Apr 2026 update (IMF-linked, constant-FX, nominal) forecasts Latin America & Caribbean total gambling GGR — all channels, onshore plus offshore — rising from $29bn in 2024 to $51bn in 2030 (~9.9% CAGR), making LatAm and Africa the fastest-growing regions globally, 'driven primarily by online channel expansion'. Global GGR crosses $1,031bn in 2030 with online at $530bn (51%).

**Regulated online was the engine.** Vixio's Latin America Outlook (Dec 2024) projected regulated online GGR growing five-fold from $2.5bn (2024) to $12.3bn (2028), with Brazil $2.9bn in 2025 (47% of the region) rising to $6.3bn (>50%) by 2028; Mexico $1.3bn→>$2bn, Colombia >$1bn, Peru $436m→>$850m. Vixio's Americas total (US, Canada, LatAm) goes from $22.3bn (2023) to $56.3bn (2028), 20.3% CAGR.

**GVR sizes LatAm online at $7.24bn in 2025** (8.3% of global online), growing 10.7% CAGR 2026–33 to $16.2bn — implying ~$12.0bn in 2030 (our arithmetic). Sports betting is both the largest and fastest-growing product; Brazil the highest-CAGR country. Note the definitional gap: Brazil's regulated GGR alone (R$36.9bn, ~$7.2bn) roughly equals GVR's entire regional figure.

**Brazil beat every forecast — then banned itself.** SPA-MF reported regulated fixed-odds GGR of R$36.9bn (~$7.2bn) in the first year of regulation (2025), >2x Vixio's $2.9bn forecast; H1 2026 GGR was R$20.07bn (~$3.9bn), +15.3% YoY (~R$3.3bn/month), with 15.1m unique CPFs betting in Q1 2026 (GGR R$7.6bn, ~$1.5bn).

**MP 1.394/2026 (25 Sep 2026) is the single largest swing factor for 2030.** The provisional measure ends the exploitation, offer, intermediation and advertising of fixed-odds betting — sports and online games, physical and virtual — including state/DF authorisations. New deposits banned from 25 Sep; sites and apps offline from 6 Oct; balances returned via banks 9–14 Oct, then Caixa. No compensation for lost profits, investment or the R$30m (~$5.9m) outorgas — 85 outorgas totalling R$2.55bn (~$0.5bn).

**Enforcement is being hard-wired.** Fines up to R$2bn (~$0.39bn), domain blocking, app removal, payment-rail restriction and account blocking; a Casa Civil-led inter-ministerial committee; a companion bill creating five crimes (4–6 years for operating fixed-odds betting; 2–4 years for advertising, data-driven acquisition, financial facilitation or hosting). Anatel had already blocked 15,463 sites (Oct 2024–Jun 2025) and ~25,000 by end-2025; 37 fintechs were notified in Jul 2026 for moving illegal-bet money.

**Brazil's pre-ban tax regime** was 12% of GGR (Law 14.790/2023) plus ordinary corporate taxes; the Jun 2025 MP 1.303 to lift the rate to 18% collapsed in Oct 2025 after a retroactive-tax rewrite. Treasury now loses ~R$800m (~$157m) per month of bet-related revenue, per press estimates — a fiscal incentive to re-regulate at a higher rate rather than prohibit indefinitely.

**Political direction: prohibition framed as public health.** Government cites +140% growth in SUS gambling-related care (2018–25), a projected +104% by 2028 and an IEPS study putting the annual social cost at R$38.8bn (~$7.6bn), R$30.6bn of it health-related. Congress has 120 days to vote the MP; trade-press headlines report Lula's re-election in Oct 2026, so a reversal by a new administration is off the table — the courts (STF) and Congress are the only routes back [post-25 Sep status unverified in this session].

**Grey market absorbs the demand.** Brazil's Central Bank estimated up to R$30bn (~$5.9bn) wagered per month in Q1 2025 across licensed and unlicensed sites; Blask tracked 523 Brazil-facing brands in Aug 2026. H2 counts offshore GGR in its totals, so the $51bn regional number is less affected than the onshore share — which we expect to fall from ~45% globally-equivalent levels to well below 40% in LatAm.

**Colombia — mature, over-taxed.** Coljuegos reported 14 authorised online operators at end-2025 (down from high-teens); exploitation rights 15% of GGR (17% if RTP <83%) [not re-verified], plus a 19% VAT on online gambling deposits imposed Feb 2025 under an economic-emergency decree; Fecoljuegos says online income fell 32%, while Coljuegos credits online VAT with ~COP 900bn (~$239m) for the Catatumbo region by Nov 2025. Vixio still sees >$1bn GGR by 2028.

**Peru — the cleanest licensing template.** Law 31557 (Aug 2022, amended by Law 31806) makes MINCETUR the licensing, supervisory and sanctioning authority; tax is 12% on net income (SUNAT); 145 applications became 118 licences for 63 operators (Dec 2024) and >60 authorised companies by Apr 2026; crypto payments are prohibited. Vixio: $436m (2025) → >$850m (2028).

**Mexico — large but legally fragile.** Vixio: $1.3bn (2024) → >$2bn (2028). SEGOB permits under the 1947 Federal Gaming Law; disputes over land-based permit renewals and online restrictions persist; a federal IEPS increase on gaming for 2026 was reported [unverified in this session].

**Argentina & Chile — patchwork and pending.** Argentina licenses online province-by-province (CABA, Buenos Aires Province and ~10 others) with a federal online-betting tax layered on provincial GGR levies [rates n/a]; Vixio flags 'potential advertising bans'. Chile has no licensing regime: a Jul 2026 study puts 2025 online GGR above $460m, with the licensing bill in the Senate since Dec 2023 [status unverified].

**Online poker — the lead release.** GVR (research commissioned by Ignition Casino, an offshore brand) sizes LatAm online poker at $261.6m (2024), 6.8% of global, rising to $467.6m by 2030 (10.2% CAGR); desktop is the largest and fastest-growing device segment. Global poker goes $3.9bn → $6.9bn. The sponsor is itself a tell: LatAm poker liquidity sits offshore.

**Payments are the regulatory lever.** Pix is 'part of the product' in Brazil (Blask) and the MP explicitly targets payment rails; Peru's law bars cryptocurrency; Colombia taxes the deposit, not the GGR. Any LatAm stack must support instant-payment rails plus regulator-grade transaction reporting (Brazil's SIGAP precedent).

**Advertising and RG tightening everywhere.** Brazil: PL 2.985/2023 (Senate-approved 28 May 2025) would restrict ad timing and sports-broadcast exposure — now overtaken by a blanket advertising/sponsorship ban under the MP, extending to placements abroad; a federal self-exclusion platform exists; health services will actively contact bettors. Peru mandates deposit limits and self-exclusion; Argentina's ad-restriction bill is pending.

**Forecast dispersion is wide — use the right definition.** H2 ($51bn total 2030), Vixio ($12.3bn regulated online 2028), GVR ($7.24bn online 2025), IMGL (>$37bn total 2025; $10–12bn online 2028) and Bradesco BBI ($17bn Brazil 2025, which BNLData says overstates SPA data 2.5x) measure different perimeters. We anchor on H2 for total GGR and Vixio/SPA for regulated online.

**Read-through for B2Tech.** Do not underwrite Brazilian regulated revenue until the MP's fate is decided; prioritise Peru, Colombia (post-VAT economics), Mexico and Argentine provinces; model GGR-equivalent tax of 12–30%+ with upward drift; build for instant-payment rails and regulator reporting; keep B2B (platform/content/payments) optionality that survives jurisdictional shocks.

**Our 2030 view (estimates).** Ban case: LatAm regulated online GGR ~$6–8bn in 2030 with total GGR near H2's $51bn but onshore share <40%. Reversal case (Brazil re-licensed by 2027 at ≥15–18% GGR tax): regulated online ~$17–20bn. The probability-weighted outcome sits well below the pre-ban consensus.

segments.name: Regional outlook to 2030 — forecast houses, definitions and scenarios
segments.headline: Every published 2030 number pre-dates Brazil's prohibition; the honest range for regulated online in 2030 is now ~$6–8bn (ban case) to ~$17–20bn (reversal case).
narrative: H2 Gambling Capital's 30 April 2026 model update, which folds in the IMF's April 2026 World Economic Outlook, is the only regional series that covers every channel and both onshore and offshore supply. It puts Latin America & the Caribbean at $29bn of GGR in 2024 and $51bn in 2030, a compound rate of roughly 9.9%, and names LatAm and Africa as the two fastest-growing regions, with growth 'driven primarily by online channel expansion'. Two caveats matter for a 2030 plan. First, H2 forecasts in local currency and translates at a constant FX rate, so the $51bn does not absorb future BRL, ARS or COP devaluation — on a current-FX basis H2 itself says the USD figures would be lower. Second, the series is nominal; in high-inflation Argentina a material share of growth is price, not volume.

Vixio's Latin America Outlook (December 2024) measures a narrower perimeter — regulated online only — and had it rising from $2.5bn in 2024 to $12.3bn in 2028, with Brazil contributing $2.9bn in 2025 (47% of the region) and $6.3bn in 2028 (over half). Mexico was forecast at $1.3bn (2024) rising above $2bn, Colombia above $1bn by 2028, and Peru from $436m (2025) to more than $850m (2028). Vixio's May 2025 Americas update put combined US, Canada and LatAm regulated online GGR at $56.3bn by 2028 (20.3% CAGR from $22.3bn in 2023), drawing level with Europe. Brazil's actual 2025 regulated GGR of R$36.9bn (~$7.2bn) was more than double Vixio's $2.9bn, so the regulated regional total for 2025 was probably in the $10–11bn range (our estimate), not the ~$6bn Vixio's path implied — the region was running well ahead of consensus before the ban.

Grand View Research's databook (28 April 2026) is the third reference point: LatAm online gambling revenue of $7.24bn in 2025, 8.3% of global online, growing at 10.7% a year from 2026 to $16.2bn in 2033, which implies about $12.0bn in 2030 on our arithmetic. Sports betting is the largest and fastest-growing product and Brazil the highest-CAGR country. GVR's figure cannot be reconciled with SPA-MF data — Brazil's regulated GGR alone roughly equals GVR's regional total — so it should be read as a lower-bound, revenue-to-operator definition rather than GGR. IMGL's summary (combined LatAm gambling revenue above $37bn in 2025; online $10–12bn by 2028) and Bradesco BBI's $17bn Brazil 2025 estimate (which BNLData shows overstates SPA-reported GGR by ~2.5x by counting grey-market flow) complete the dispersion. For planning we anchor total GGR on H2 and regulated online on the regulators' own series plus Vixio.

None of these models incorporates MP 1.394/2026. On our arithmetic, Brazil was roughly half of regulated LatAm online GGR and the majority of its forecast growth. We therefore frame 2030 as two scenarios rather than a point estimate. In the ban case (the MP is converted into law or re-issued and survives the courts), regulated online GGR ex-Brazil compounds from the ~$3.5–4bn 2025 base across Mexico, Colombia, Peru, Argentina's provinces and others to roughly $6–8bn by 2030 (estimate), with Chile adding perhaps $0.3–0.5bn only if its bill passes by 2028. Brazilian demand does not disappear: with the Central Bank already measuring up to R$30bn (~$5.9bn) of monthly wagering in Q1 2025 and Blask tracking 523 Brazil-facing brands in August 2026, offshore GGR of $6–9bn in 2030 is plausible (estimate), keeping H2's total near $51bn but collapsing the onshore share. In the reversal case (the MP lapses, is rejected or is suspended by the STF and Brazil re-licenses during 2027 at a higher rate, most likely 15–18% of GGR plus ad limits), Brazil's regulated GGR could reach R$55–65bn (~$11–13bn at constant FX) by 2030 and regional regulated online ~$17–20bn (estimate). We weight the ban case more heavily for 2027–28 and see a partial re-opening as the more probable end-state by 2030, because the fiscal loss (~R$800m, ~$157m per month) and the enforcement burden of a wholly offshore market are hard for any administration to sustain.

segments.name: Brazil — from flagship to prohibition
segments.headline: R$36.9bn (~$7.2bn) of regulated GGR in year one, +15.3% in H1 2026, then a presidential provisional measure that switched the market off on 6 Oct 2026 without compensation.
narrative: Brazil's framework rested on Law 13.756/2018 (which created fixed-odds betting as a lottery modality) and Law 14.790/2023, which set the operating rules, a 12% levy on GGR, a R$30m (~$5.9m) five-year authorisation fee covering up to three brands, and the Secretaria de Prêmios e Apostas (SPA-MF) inside the Ministry of Finance as regulator; the licensed market went live on 1 January 2025. Uptake exceeded every forecast: SPA-MF's SIGAP data show regulated GGR of R$17.4bn (~$3.4bn) in H1 2025, R$36.9bn (~$7.2bn) for full-year 2025, and R$20.07bn (~$3.9bn) in H1 2026, up 15.3% year on year at an average of ~R$3.3bn (~$0.65bn) per month (Sigma reports R$20.28bn and +6.2% for the same period — the growth-rate gap reflects differing H1 2025 baselines and we quote the SPA-sourced BNLData series). In Q1 2026 alone 15.1m unique CPFs placed bets, generating R$7.6bn (~$1.5bn) — roughly R$168 (~$33) of GGR per active bettor per quarter. Authorised companies grew from 82 (March 2026) to 84 by mid-year and 85 outorgas by September, carrying roughly 186–188 brands, and the fees paid totalled R$2.55bn (~$0.5bn).

The tax environment was already in flux before the ban. The 12% GGR contribution sits on top of ordinary PIS/COFINS, ISS and corporate income taxes, and the player pays income tax on net winnings [structure per Law 14.790; rates not re-verified in this session]. In June 2025 the government published MP 1.303/2025 to lift the GGR rate to 18%; after the Chamber rewrote it into a retroactive model in early October 2025 the measure collapsed without a vote, leaving 12% in place. Press reports also reference a scheduled glide-path to 15% by 2028 (+1pp a year in 2026–27) [unverified]. Enforcement, by contrast, was effective and escalating: Anatel blocked 15,463 unlicensed domains between October 2024 and June 2025 and about 25,000 by end-2025; 229 illegal influencer posts were removed in 2025; in July 2026 the government notified 37 fintechs for processing illegal-bet money. Advertising was being tightened in parallel through PL 2.985/2023, approved by the Senate on 28 May 2025, which would bar ads during live sports broadcasts and restrict ad windows.

On 25 September 2026 President Lula signed MP 1.394/2026, which — on public-health grounds — ends the exploitation, offer, intermediation and advertising of fixed-odds betting in Brazil, covering sports betting and online games in both physical and virtual channels, and extinguishing state and Federal District authorisations as well as the 85 federal ones. The timetable was compressed: new deposits banned from publication; voluntary withdrawals until 23:59 on 5 October; sites and apps offline on 6 October; operators to report residual balances by CPF to banks on 7–8 October; banks to refund 9–14 October, with Caixa Econômica Federal as the fallback paying agent. Operators get no indemnity for lost profits, sunk investment, expectation of continuity or the outorga fees. Sanctions run from warnings to fines of up to R$2bn (~$0.39bn) and partial or total suspension, and a Casa Civil-coordinated committee will drive domain blocking, app removal, payment-method restriction, account freezes and fund tracing. A companion bill would create five crimes: 4–6 years' imprisonment for exploiting fixed-odds betting and 2–4 years plus fines for advertising or acquiring bettors, using personal data to do so, financially facilitating the activity, or hosting it — with aggravation where health data, betting histories, minors' data or circumvented age/geolocation checks are involved. The government's evidence base is a reported 140% rise in SUS gambling-related care between 2018 and 2025, a projected further 104% by 2028, and an IEPS estimate of R$38.8bn (~$7.6bn) in annual social cost, R$30.6bn of it health-related; the Health Ministry will actively contact former bettors. The MP has immediate effect but Congress must convert it within 120 days (i.e. by late January 2027), and the criminalisation bill needs separate passage.

For an operator the implications are stark. Roughly half of Latin America's regulated online GGR and the majority of its forecast growth are now, at best, a 2027–28 re-entry option. Capital already committed — licence fees, Brazilian entities, SIGAP integrations, Pix acquiring, sports sponsorships — is impaired, and the MP's refusal of compensation makes any recovery a judicial question. Trade-press headlines report Lula's re-election in October 2026, so a change of administration is not a path to reversal; the live routes are a congressional rejection or amendment of the MP, an STF suspension on constitutional grounds (the 2024 PGR action against Law 14.790 shows the Court is already seised of the framework), or a negotiated re-regulation at a materially higher tax rate once the fiscal hole (~R$800m, ~$157m per month, per InfoMoney) bites. Until one of those crystallises, Brazil should be modelled as an offshore market with aggressive payment and domain enforcement, and any Brazil-facing activity should be assessed against the proposed criminal exposure for operators, payment facilitators and hosts — including the extraterritorial reach of the advertising ban.

segments.name: Colombia, Peru, Chile & Argentina — the Andean and Southern Cone regulated pool
segments.headline: Colombia's VAT and Peru's licensing wave define the ex-Brazil opportunity; Chile is still unlicensed and Argentina is a provincial patchwork with an ad-ban overhang.
narrative: Colombia remains the region's longest-running regulated online market — Coljuegos has licensed internet operators since 2016 under Law 643/2001 — but it is now the clearest case study in fiscal over-reach. Coljuegos' own data show 14 authorised online operators at the end of 2025, down from the high-teens of 2023–24, after the government used a February 2025 economic-emergency decree (the Catatumbo crisis) to impose 19% VAT on online gambling, levied on player deposits rather than GGR, on top of exploitation rights of 15% of GGR (17% where RTP is below 83%) [exploitation-rights rates per Coljuegos rules, not re-verified in this session]. Fecoljuegos reports online income down 32% following the VAT, whereas Coljuegos presents the same measure as a success, crediting online games with roughly COP 900bn (~$239m) of VAT for the Catatumbo region plus COP 46bn (~$12.2m) of exploitation rights by November 2025. Whether the VAT survives beyond its emergency legal basis depends on the Constitutional Court and Congress [status at Nov 2026 unverified]. Vixio still projects Colombian GGR above $1bn by 2028. For an entrant the market is attractive for its depth, regulator maturity and payment infrastructure, but the deposit-based VAT structurally punishes high-turnover, low-margin sportsbook and makes bonus-led acquisition uneconomic; the leading incumbents (BetPlay, Wplay, Rushbet and the Codere/Betsson/Stake brands [shares n/a]) have scale advantages that a new licensee cannot buy with promotions.

Peru is the model the rest of the region is copying. Law 31557 (August 2022), amended by Law 31806 (June 2023) and operational from February 2024, makes MINCETUR the national authority that regulates, authorises, revokes, supervises and sanctions remote gaming and remote sports betting; SUNAT administers a 12% tax on net income from platforms authorised by MINCETUR, and the law requires that bets be funded with cash, cards or other approved means but expressly excludes cryptocurrencies. The first window drew 145 applications, Vixio recorded 118 licences issued to 63 operators by December 2024, and Focus Gaming News counted more than 60 authorised companies in April 2026. Vixio forecasts $436m of GGR in 2025 rising above $850m by 2028. Licensed operators must offer deposit limits and self-exclusion. A selective-consumption tax on each wager was reported from 2025 [rate unverified in this session] and would be an incremental turnover-based drag. The commercial read is that Peru is open, competitive and reasonably taxed; the risk is crowding — more than 60 licensees in a sub-$1bn market implies consolidation and rising acquisition costs rather than regulatory shock.

Chile has demand without a regime. A July 2026 study reported by Yogonet estimates Chilean online GGR above $460m in 2025, all of it unlicensed, with the fiscal leakage from unauthorised play put at ~CLP 86bn (~$92.6m). The online gambling bill cleared the Chamber of Deputies in December 2023 and has been in the Senate since; it envisages a GGR-based tax, a licensing regime administered by the Superintendencia de Casinos de Juego, and a cooling-off period for operators active in the grey market [bill terms not re-verified; passage timing unverified]. Vixio expected a framework 'by 2025', which has not happened. We would not plan for licensed Chilean revenue before 2028, and we would treat grey-market exposure as a licensing liability given the bill's blackout provisions and the SCJ's litigation record against offshore brands.

Argentina regulates online gambling province by province. Buenos Aires City (LOTBA) and Buenos Aires Province (IPLyC) launched licensed online markets in 2021–22 and have since been joined by roughly ten other provinces [count unverified], each with its own tax base and rate [rates n/a], while a federal indirect tax applies to online bets with a surcharge for operators without local presence [rates n/a]. Vixio's principal warning is 'potential advertising bans': a national bill restricting betting advertising and access has been advancing through Congress [status unverified]. Hyper-inflation and currency controls make USD-denominated forecasts unreliable, which is why Vixio and H2 give no clean Argentine GGR line we can quote. Argentina is best approached through established provincial licensees (Boldt, Codere, Betsson, bet365 and the Buenos Aires casino groups) as a B2B supplier rather than as a licence-holder, with ARS-denominated commercial terms.

segments.name: Mexico, Central America & the Caribbean
segments.headline: Mexico is the second-largest regulated pool (>$2bn by 2028) but runs on a 1947 statute and discretionary permits; the smaller Central American and Caribbean regimes are niche licensing bases rather than demand markets.
narrative: Mexico is the one large LatAm market whose growth path Vixio did not condition on new legislation: $1.3bn of online GGR in 2024 rising above $2bn by 2028. Operators work under the Federal Law on Games and Raffles of 1947 and its 2004 regulation, with permits issued and policed by SEGOB's Dirección General de Juegos y Sorteos; online offerings are typically run under an existing land-based permit-holder's authorisation rather than a standalone online licence [structure per long-standing practice, not re-verified in this session]. Vixio flags 'regulatory challenges tied to land-based operator licenses and disputes over online gaming restrictions' — a reference to the November 2023 presidential decree curbing slot machines and new permits, and to contested permit renewals. Tax is the federal IEPS on gaming, historically 30% of gross receipts, with state levies layered on top; an increase for 2026 was reported in the budget package [unverified in this session]. The market is concentrated around Caliente, with Codere, PlayCity, Big Bola, Strendus and the international brands behind them [shares n/a]. For an entrant, Mexico offers scale and a mature cash-voucher and bank-transfer payment stack, but it is a permit-partnership market where access depends on an incumbent's goodwill and where the legal base can move by decree rather than statute.

The smaller jurisdictions matter mainly as licensing bases and as early signals of regional policy. Panama's Junta de Control de Juegos licenses online sportsbooks; Costa Rica hosts offshore operators under data-processing licences rather than gambling licences; Paraguay replaced its monopoly model with a new licensing law in 2024 [details unverified]; Ecuador introduced taxation of betting operators and prizes in 2024 and is drafting a regulatory framework [unverified]; Uruguay retains a state monopoly for online betting. Puerto Rico and the Dominican Republic have US-style or hybrid frameworks. None of these is likely to exceed a few hundred million dollars of GGR by 2030, but Panama and Costa Rica are relevant to any decision on where to domicile a Brazil-facing offshore operation — a decision that, after MP 1.394/2026, carries explicit criminal and payments-enforcement risk.

segments.name: Licensing & tax matrix — how the rules compare
segments.headline: GGR-based levies of 12–15% were the regional norm; the trend since 2025 is to add turnover- or deposit-based layers (Colombia VAT, Peru ISC) or to prohibit outright (Brazil).
narrative: The region's licensing architecture is converging on the Peruvian/Brazilian template — a national authority, a fixed-fee multi-year authorisation, local-entity and reporting requirements — while the tax architecture is diverging. Brazil's Law 14.790/2023 priced entry at R$30m (~$5.9m) for five years and up to three brands, with a 12% levy on GGR; Peru charges 12% on net income; Colombia 15% of GGR (17% below an 83% RTP) [not re-verified]; Mexico applies IEPS on gross receipts at 30% [2026 increase unverified]; Argentina stacks provincial GGR taxes on a federal online-bet tax [rates n/a]. The direction since early 2025 has been unambiguously upward: Colombia's 19% VAT on deposits, Peru's reported wager-level ISC, Brazil's attempted (failed) 12%→18% hike and reported 15%-by-2028 glide path, and the Mexican IEPS proposal. The Colombian experience — 14 licensees and a reported 32% fall in online income after the VAT — is the empirical warning that deposit- or turnover-based taxes bite far harder than their headline rate suggests, because they are levied on stake recycling rather than margin.

Licence counts tell the same story from the supply side. Brazil moved from 114 applications (late 2024) to 85 authorised companies and ~188 brands by September 2026, then to zero. Peru moved from 145 applications to 118 licences for 63 operators and still counts more than 60 authorised companies. Colombia has drifted down to 14. For B2Tech the implication is that licence availability is not the constraint — Peru and Brazil both showed regulators willing to license almost every credible applicant — but licence durability is. Brazil's extinguishment of 85 authorisations without refund of R$2.55bn (~$0.5bn) of fees is the most severe regulatory expropriation in a licensed online market anywhere, and it will be priced into every LatAm licence by lenders and boards. Structures that keep technology, content and payments contracts separable from the licensed entity, and that avoid front-loading multi-year fees, are now a governance requirement rather than a preference.

segments.name: Payments, responsible gambling, advertising & enforcement
segments.headline: Instant-payment rails made LatAm online gambling scale; regulators have now learned to use the same rails — and advertising law — as the enforcement perimeter.
narrative: Payments explain both the speed of LatAm's growth and the shape of its enforcement. In Brazil, Pix — the Central Bank's instant rail — is, in Blask's phrase, 'part of the product': it enabled the 15.1m-bettor quarter in Q1 2026 and the up-to-R$30bn (~$5.9bn) monthly wagering the Central Bank measured in Q1 2025. The same rail is now the enforcement tool. MP 1.394/2026 directs the Finance and Justice ministries to restrict payment methods, block accounts used illegally and trace platform flows, and the government had already notified 37 fintechs in July 2026 over illegal-bet money; iGaming Brazil reports Central Bank data showing a nationwide decline in Pix transactions that began before the ban. Peru's law lists acceptable funding methods and expressly excludes cryptocurrency; Colombia's VAT is collected at the deposit, which makes the payment processor the tax-collection point; Mexico relies on OXXO cash vouchers and SPEI transfers, and Argentina on bank transfers and wallets such as Mercado Pago [Mexico/Argentina payment mix per market practice, not re-verified]. A LatAm platform must therefore be built around regulator-grade transaction reporting (Brazil's SIGAP daily feed is the precedent) and be able to switch rails quickly when a regulator restricts one.

Responsible-gambling obligations have hardened from product features into public-health policy. Brazil's pre-ban regime already required a federal self-exclusion platform (gov.br/autoexclusaoapostas), advertising rules barring appeals to minors and misleading claims, and a ban on credit-card funding [credit-card rule per Law 14.790, not re-verified]; the MP goes further by framing prohibition as a health intervention, citing +140% growth in SUS gambling-related care (2018–25) and an IEPS social-cost estimate of R$38.8bn (~$7.6bn) a year, and by instructing the health system to actively seek out former bettors. Peru requires deposit limits and self-exclusion as licence conditions. Colombia's Coljuegos and Argentina's provincial lotteries run self-exclusion registers [not re-verified]. The practical read is that LatAm regulators now treat problem-gambling statistics as a licensing-policy input, not just a compliance checkbox, so operators' own affordability and intervention data will become a political asset or liability.

Advertising is the second enforcement perimeter. Brazil's PL 2.985/2023, approved by the Senate on 28 May 2025 over the objections of operators and football clubs, would prohibit betting ads during live sports broadcasts and confine them to limited windows; the MP overtakes it with a complete ban on advertising, marketing and sponsorship of fixed-odds betting, including placements abroad, with 2–4 years' imprisonment proposed for advertising or data-driven customer acquisition. Argentina's national advertising bill and Vixio's warning of 'potential advertising bans' show the same direction, and Colombia and Peru already restrict content and bonus messaging. On the enforcement side, Brazil's Anatel blocked 15,463 unlicensed sites in the first nine months of regulation and ~25,000 by end-2025, removed 229 illegal influencer posts in 2025, and will now apply the same machinery to former licensees; Coljuegos has run domain-blocking since 2017; Chile's SCJ has pursued offshore operators through the courts. The practical conclusion for an operator is that affiliate-, influencer- and sponsorship-led growth models — the ones that built Brazil's R$36.9bn year — are the most exposed to the region's next regulatory wave, and that media-rights and club-sponsorship commitments should carry regulatory-change termination rights.

segments.name: Online poker — the lead release in context
segments.headline: A $467.6m niche by 2030 (10.2% CAGR), 6.8% of global poker, sized by research an offshore brand commissioned — which is itself the point.
narrative: The release that prompted this brief is Grand View Research's Latin America online poker databook (published 13 May 2025), re-circulated in October 2026 as research commissioned by Ignition Casino. It puts LatAm online poker revenue at $261.6m in 2024 — 6.8% of a $3.9bn global market — rising at 10.2% a year from 2025 to $467.6m in 2030, while global poker reaches $4.7bn in 2026 and $6.9bn in 2030 on the same CAGR. Desktop is reported as both the largest and the fastest-growing device segment, an unusual profile for a mobile-first region that points to a tournament- and cash-game player base rather than casual mobile play. The sponsor's commentary cites rising search interest in Argentina, Mexico, Chile and Peru.

Set against the regulated frameworks, the poker forecast is almost entirely an offshore number. Brazil — poker's largest LatAm base by population and by live-tournament activity — never carved out a ring-fenced poker regime within Law 14.790 and is now prohibited outright; Colombia's VAT on deposits is punitive for rake-based products; Peru's 12% regime permits poker but liquidity is thin; Mexico and Argentina's provinces license poker under general online permits but pool liquidity only with international networks. That a Costa Rica-based, grey-market brand is the one commissioning the research is consistent with H2's observation that offshore operators still hold 55% of global online GGR. For B2Tech, poker is not a licence-led entry product in LatAm; it is a liquidity-network decision, and the 2030 figure of $467.6m should be treated as the size of a market that regulated operators will mostly not be able to address unless Brazil re-opens with a poker-compatible regime.

highlights.text: Structural demand is proven, not theoretical: Brazil generated R$36.9bn (~$7.2bn) of regulated GGR in its first year — more than double Vixio's forecast — with 15.1m unique bettors in a single quarter; that demand persists whatever the licensing status, and H2 still models LatAm total GGR rising to $51bn by 2030.

Peru offers a clean, open licensing template: MINCETUR has authorised >60 companies, tax is 12% of net income, and Vixio sees GGR doubling to >$850m by 2028 — a low-friction base for a B2B platform/content play.

Mexico is the largest regulated pool unaffected by new legislation (>$2bn online GGR by 2028, Vixio), with a mature cash-voucher and bank-transfer payment stack; permit partnerships with incumbents are the entry route.

Chile's >$460m of unlicensed online GGR (2025) is an identifiable licensing prize once the Senate bill passes; early compliance positioning (no grey-market exposure) is the way to be eligible on day one.

Brazil's fiscal hole (~R$800m / ~$157m per month of lost federal revenue) and the enforcement cost of a wholly offshore market create a credible path to re-regulation at a higher tax rate by 2027–28 — a re-entry option for operators who preserve Brazilian entities, data and relationships.

Online poker and other liquidity products ($467.6m by 2030, GVR) favour network operators; a B2B supplier positioned across Argentine provinces, Mexico and Peru can aggregate liquidity that single-market licensees cannot.
Regulators across the region (SPA-MF's SIGAP, Coljuegos, MINCETUR) now demand daily transaction-level reporting — a compliance-technology moat for suppliers who already run it.

lowlights.text: Brazil's MP 1.394/2026 is the most severe regulatory expropriation in any licensed online market: 85 authorisations extinguished from 6 Oct 2026, R$2.55bn (~$0.5bn) of fees forfeited, no compensation for sunk investment, fines up to R$2bn (~$0.39bn) and proposed 4–6-year prison terms for operators — roughly half of regional regulated online GGR removed.

Tax drift is upward and shifting to turnover/deposit bases: Colombia's 19% VAT on deposits coincided with a reported 32% fall in online income and a licensee count down to 14; Peru added a wager-level ISC [unverified]; Brazil attempted 12%→18%; Mexico's IEPS rise was reported for 2026 [unverified].

Every published 2030 forecast (H2 $51bn total; Vixio $12.3bn regulated online 2028; GVR $7.24bn→$16.2bn) pre-dates the Brazilian ban and the models disagree on perimeter by a factor of 2–7x; capital plans built on these numbers are mis-specified.

Advertising prohibition is spreading: Brazil's MP bans all betting advertising and sponsorship (even placed abroad) with criminal penalties proposed; PL 2.985/2023 and Argentina's national bill show the same direction — affiliate-, influencer- and sponsorship-led growth models are the most exposed.

Payment rails are now an enforcement perimeter: Brazil is restricting payment methods and freezing accounts, notified 37 fintechs in Jul 2026, and Pix volumes were already falling; PSP and acquiring partners carry legal exposure for any Brazil-facing flows.

Political timing is unfavourable to reversal: Congress has only 120 days to vote the MP, trade-press headlines report Lula's re-election in Oct 2026, and the public-health framing (R$38.8bn / ~$7.6bn social cost; +140% SUS care) gives prohibition broad cover; STF litigation is slow and uncertain [post-25 Sep status unverified].

FX and inflation erode USD economics: H2's forecasts are constant-FX, and Argentina's and Brazil's currencies have a record of devaluation; USD-reported growth will lag local-currency growth, and licence fees paid in local currency (R$30m) are hard to recover.

forecast.intro: The pre-ban consensus had Latin America as the world's fastest-growing regulated region: H2 Gambling Capital's April 2026 update takes total GGR from $29bn (2024) to $51bn (2030), Vixio takes regulated online from $2.5bn (2024) to $12.3bn (2028), and GVR's online series implies ~$12bn by 2030 with poker at $467.6m. Brazil drove the bridge in every model — Vixio had it at 47% of regulated online in 2025 rising to over half by 2028, and actual SPA-MF data (R$36.9bn / ~$7.2bn in 2025; R$20.07bn / ~$3.9bn in H1 2026, +15.3%) ran more than twice ahead of that path. MP 1.394/2026 reverses the bridge: from 6 Oct 2026 Brazil contributes zero regulated GGR, and the moving parts for 2030 are (i) whether Congress converts, amends or lets the MP lapse within 120 days, (ii) whether the STF suspends it, (iii) the tax rate and advertising regime attached to any re-licensing, and (iv) how much Brazilian demand the offshore market retains under payment-rail enforcement. Outside Brazil the bridge is intact but slower: Colombia's VAT has cut licensee numbers to 14, Peru is crowding, Mexico's permit regime is discretionary, Chile's bill remains unpassed and Argentina faces an advertising bill.

B2Tech 2030 regulated online — ban case / reversal case (est.)

forecast.view: Our independent view is that **the 2030 regulated market will be materially smaller than the published consensus and more fragmented**. Base case (ban persists through 2027, partial Brazilian re-licensing from 2028 at a 15–18% GGR levy with a blanket sports-sponsorship ban): LatAm regulated online GGR of roughly **$10–13bn in 2030** (estimate), ex-Brazil regulated online compounding at ~12–15% a year to ~$6–8bn, Brazil regulated contributing ~$4–5bn in a first partial year, and offshore Brazilian GGR of $5–8bn persisting despite enforcement. H2's $51bn total-GGR figure remains plausible because it includes offshore and land-based (lotteries, Mexican and Argentine casinos), but the onshore online share of LatAm GGR falls rather than rises. **Margins compress**: effective tax on GGR-equivalent terms moves from ~12–15% to 20–30%+ across Colombia (VAT), Mexico (IEPS) and a re-licensed Brazil, and acquisition costs rise as advertising windows close — expect EBITDA margins for licensed sportsbook operators in the low-to-mid teens, with casino content and B2B suppliers retaining better economics. **Leverage and capital intensity rise**: licence fees become sunk and non-recoverable risks, so boards will demand shorter payback, local-currency debt and separable B2B structures. Swing factors, in order of importance: the fate of MP 1.394/2026 in Congress (by late Jan 2027) and at the STF; Colombia's Constitutional Court/Congress decision on the permanence of the 19% VAT; passage of Chile's bill; Mexico's 2026 IEPS treatment; and Argentina's advertising bill. Upside to our base case comes from a quick Brazilian reversal; downside from Mexico or Colombia following Brazil's public-health framing.
watch: Brazil: Congress vote on MP 1.394/2026 within 120 days (by ~late Jan 2027); STF actions on the MP and the 2024 PGR challenge to Law 14.790; progress of the five-crime bill; any Finance Ministry signal on re-licensing at 15–18% of GGR.
Brazil: Central Bank Pix volume data and Anatel blocking statistics as a proxy for offshore migration; monthly federal revenue shortfall (~R$800m / ~$157m) in Receita Federal releases.
Colombia: Constitutional Court and Congress decisions on the 19% VAT on online gambling deposits; Coljuegos licensee count (14 at end-2025) and quarterly exploitation-rights collections.
Peru: MINCETUR licence renewals/revocations among >60 authorised companies; SUNAT collections under the 12% regime and the reported wager-level ISC.
Chile: Senate committee timetable for the online gambling bill; SCJ litigation against offshore brands; whether the 2025 >$460m unlicensed GGR estimate is adopted in the fiscal case for passage.
Mexico: 2026 IEPS treatment of gaming and SEGOB permit renewals; any move to a standalone online licence.
